marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q008.takeaway: The most caudal right posterior cardinal vein contributes to the right common iliac vein; the left common iliac vein develops from the sacrocardinal anastomosis.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q008.displayText: The posterior cardinal venous system contributes to the common iliac region. In particular, the most caudal portion of the right posterior cardinal vein persists as part of the right common iliac vein. The left common iliac vein is formed differently, from the anastomosis between the sacrocardinal veins. By contrast, the superior vena cava and internal jugular veins are principally derivatives of the anterior/common cardinal system. Therefore the adult structure linked to the posterior cardinal vein here is the common iliac vein.
emphasis: most caudal portion of the right posterior cardinal vein

rationales.b: The superior vena cava develops mainly from the right common cardinal vein and proximal right anterior cardinal vein, not the posterior cardinal vein.
rationales.c: The internal jugular veins derive from the cranial portions of the anterior cardinal veins rather than the posterior cardinal system.
rationales.d: The external jugular vein is not the posterior-cardinal derivative tested here; the relevant persistent caudal derivative is the common iliac vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q009.takeaway: Vitelline veins contribute to the hepatic, portal, hepatocardiac IVC, and superior mesenteric venous systems; the superior vena cava is cardinal-vein derived.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q009.displayText: The superior vena cava is not a vitelline-vein derivative. Vitelline veins run from the yolk sac toward the sinus venosus and are remodeled extensively around the developing liver and duodenum. Their derivatives include hepatic venous channels, the portal venous system, the right hepatocardiac contribution to the inferior vena cava, and the superior mesenteric vein. In contrast, the superior vena cava is formed from the right common cardinal vein together with the proximal right anterior cardinal vein. This vitelline-versus-cardinal distinction identifies the exception.
emphasis: superior vena cava is not a vitelline-vein derivative
right hepatocardiac contribution to the inferior vena cava
right common cardinal vein together with the proximal right anterior cardinal vein

rationales.a: Hepatic venous channels develop from the vitelline venous plexus within the developing liver, so hepatic vein is a vitelline derivative.
rationales.c: The hepatic/hepatocardiac segment of the inferior vena cava includes a right-vitelline contribution, so IVC is not the exception.
rationales.d: The superior mesenteric vein is derived from the right vitelline venous system and drains the midgut territory.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q010.takeaway: Ostium secundum forms in the upper part of septum primum before ostium primum closes, preserving right-to-left atrial flow in fetal life.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q010.displayText: The foramen secundum, or ostium secundum, is formed in the upper part of the septum primum. Septum primum initially grows toward the endocardial cushions, leaving the lower ostium primum. Before that first opening is completely closed, perforations develop in the upper septum primum and coalesce to create ostium secundum, maintaining interatrial flow. Septum secundum subsequently forms to the right of septum primum and leaves the foramen ovale. Therefore the location asked for is the upper part of septum primum.
emphasis: upper part of the septum primum

rationales.a: Septum secundum leaves the foramen ovale; ostium secundum itself forms within septum primum, not the upper septum secundum.
rationales.b: The lower margin of septum primum initially bounds ostium primum, not ostium secundum.
rationales.d: The lower free margin of septum secundum participates in the foramen ovale region rather than forming ostium secundum.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q011.takeaway: The limbus of the fossa ovalis is derived from septum secundum, whereas the floor of the fossa ovalis is derived from septum primum.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q011.displayText: The limbus of the fossa ovalis, also called the annulus ovalis, is the prominent rim derived from the lower free edge of septum secundum. The fossa ovalis marks the site of the fetal foramen ovale in the interatrial septum. Its thin floor is derived mainly from septum primum, while its raised limbus is a septum-secundum remnant. Keeping floor and rim separate is the key anatomical discriminator: floor equals septum primum; limbus equals septum secundum.
emphasis: lower free edge of septum secundum
floor is derived mainly from septum primum

rationales.a: Septum primum forms the thin floor of the fossa ovalis rather than its prominent limbus.
rationales.c: The floor and limbus have different embryologic origins, so both septa do not jointly form the limbus.
rationales.d: The limbus has a defined embryologic origin from septum secundum, so it is not without a listed derivative.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q012.takeaway: The membranous part of the interventricular septum is formed through endocardial-cushion contribution; the muscular septum grows from the primitive ventricle.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q012.displayText: The marked structure in the source diagram is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. This small superior portion is completed by tissue contributed through the endocardial cushions as the ventricular septal components and conotruncal region unite. Endocardial cushions also participate in atrioventricular septation, atrioventricular canal and valve formation, and outflow-tract partitioning. This is distinct from septum primum, which participates in atrial septation, and from venous-valve derivatives. Thus the image-dependent answer is endocardial cushions.
emphasis: membranous part of the interventricular septum

rationales.b: Septum primum is an atrial-septation structure and does not form the membranous interventricular septum.
rationales.c: The left venous valve contributes to venous structures in the atrial region, not the membranous interventricular septum.
rationales.d: Bulbus cordis contributes ventricular outflow and right-ventricular derivatives; it is not the source named for the marked membranous septal part.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q013.takeaway: The arch of the aorta is built from the aortic sac/left horn and left fourth aortic arch; the left second arch largely regresses.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q013.displayText: The left second aortic arch does not contribute to the definitive arch of the aorta. The aortic arch is assembled from the ventral aortic sac and its left horn together with the left fourth aortic arch; adjoining dorsal-aortic tissue contributes to the descending continuity. The first and second arch arteries largely regress, leaving only small named remnants. Therefore, among the listed structures, the left second arch artery is the non-contributor.
emphasis: left second aortic arch does not contribute

rationales.a: The left horn of the aortic sac contributes to the proximal arch region and is therefore a true contributor.
rationales.b: The left fourth aortic arch forms a major segment of the definitive aortic arch.
rationales.c: The aortic sac contributes to the proximal great-artery/arch complex and is not the exception.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q014.takeaway: The right fourth aortic arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery; the left fourth arch contributes to the aortic arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q014.displayText: The proximal segment of the right subclavian artery is derived from the right fourth aortic arch. Its more distal portions are completed by the right dorsal aorta and seventh intersegmental artery. The fourth arches persist bilaterally but have asymmetric adult fates: the left fourth arch contributes to the aortic arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, whereas the right fourth arch contributes to the proximal right subclavian artery. This side-specific fourth-arch derivative is the key discriminator.
emphasis: proximal segment of the right subclavian artery
left fourth arch contributes to the aortic arch

rationales.a: The common carotid arteries are primarily third-aortic-arch derivatives, not right fourth-arch derivatives.
rationales.c: The definitive aortic arch segment between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries is a left fourth-arch derivative, not a right fourth-arch derivative.
rationales.d: The right fourth aortic arch does not regress completely; it persists as the proximal right subclavian artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q015.takeaway: Ductus arteriosus begins functional closure almost immediately after birth, while anatomical obliteration takes roughly 2–3 weeks.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q015.displayText: The ductus arteriosus begins functional closure almost immediately after birth as its muscular wall constricts. Lung expansion raises arterial oxygen tension and placental separation reduces circulating prostaglandin support, favoring ductal constriction. Functional closure therefore precedes anatomical closure, which occurs over the following 2–3 weeks and leaves the ligamentum arteriosum. In a premature infant with a persistent ductus, a prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitor such as indomethacin can promote closure. The timing distinction tested here is immediate functional closure versus later anatomical closure.
emphasis: functional closure almost immediately after birth
immediate functional closure versus later anatomical closure

rationales.a: One to two months is much later than the normal onset of functional ductal closure after birth.
rationales.b: One to two weeks approaches the period of anatomical remodeling, not the onset of functional closure.
rationales.c: One to two days is still later than the normal beginning of functional constriction, which starts almost immediately after birth.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q016.takeaway: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failure of conotruncal ridges to form, leaving a single outflow tract that receives blood from both ventricles.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q016.displayText: The source schematic represents persistent truncus arteriosus, in which a single arterial outflow tract persists above the ventricles. The embryologic defect is failure of the conotruncal ridges to form, so the aortopulmonary septum cannot partition the truncus into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Because conotruncal tissue also participates in ventricular septation, a ventricular septal defect commonly accompanies the lesion and the common trunk receives mixed blood from both ventricles. This differs from transposition, where the septum forms but fails to spiral normally, and tetralogy of Fallot, where anterior displacement of the conotruncal septum is central.
emphasis: failure of the conotruncal ridges to form
septum forms but fails to spiral normally

rationales.a: Abnormal failure of a formed aortopulmonary septum to spiral produces transposition of the great arteries rather than persistent truncus arteriosus.
rationales.c: Anterior displacement of the conotruncal septum is the classic embryologic mechanism underlying tetralogy of Fallot.
rationales.d: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection is a pulmonary-venous developmental anomaly and does not create a single persistent arterial trunk.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q017.takeaway: Transposition of the great arteries results when the aortopulmonary septum fails to spiral, producing aorta from the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q017.displayText: An egg-on-a-string appearance in a cyanotic newborn is characteristic of transposition of the great arteries. The key embryologic error is that the aortopulmonary, or conotruncal, septum does not follow its normal spiral course and instead runs relatively straight. Consequently, the aorta connects to the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk connects to the left ventricle, creating parallel circulations that require mixing for survival. This mechanism is distinct from absent conotruncal ridges in persistent truncus arteriosus and anterior conotruncal displacement in tetralogy of Fallot.
emphasis: aortopulmonary, or conotruncal, septum does not follow its normal spiral course
aorta connects to the right ventricle
pulmonary trunk connects to the left ventricle

rationales.a: Failure of conotruncal ridge formation/fusion is associated with persistent truncus or related conotruncal septation defects rather than the non-spiraling mechanism of TGA.
rationales.c: Anterior displacement of the aortopulmonary septum is associated with tetralogy of Fallot, not transposition of the great arteries.
rationales.d: A non-fusion description does not capture the defining TGA defect; the septum is present but follows an abnormal non-spiral course.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q018.takeaway: The distal umbilical arteries obliterate after birth to form the medial umbilical ligaments; their proximal portions persist as superior vesical arteries.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q018.displayText: The marked vessel in the source umbilical-cord section is an umbilical artery. After birth, the distal portions of the umbilical arteries become obliterated and form the medial umbilical ligaments, while the proximal portions remain patent as the superior vesical arteries. Do not confuse this paired medial ligament with the median umbilical ligament, which is the urachal remnant. The left umbilical vein instead becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver. Therefore the marked umbilical artery leaves the medial umbilical ligament as its adult fibrous remnant.
emphasis: distal portions of the umbilical arteries
proximal portions remain patent as the superior vesical arteries

rationales.a: Ligamentum arteriosum is the postnatal remnant of the ductus arteriosus, not an umbilical artery.
rationales.b: Ligamentum teres of the liver is the remnant of the left umbilical vein rather than the umbilical arteries.
rationales.c: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus; the paired distal umbilical arteries form the medial umbilical ligaments.
